endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: A supplier of a mental health chatbot shall cause the mental health chatbot to clearly and conspicuously disclose to a Utah user that the mental health chatbot is an artificial intelligence technology and not a human.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, the team should determine whether the developer team incorporates a method (e.g. Model Cards) to communicate to end users the fact that they are interacting with an AI.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Document interactions with GAI systems to users prior to interactive activities, particularly in contexts involving more significant risks.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: To manage risk, health care organizations should develop and adopt appropriate polices that anticipate and minimize negative impacts.

endorsements.title: Preparing AI chatbots to respond to patient distress and suicidality in high-risk healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: (1) intentionally building safety guardrails into the chatbot architecture, including templated safety disclaimers (e.g., encouraging 911/988 call for an emergency) output to users upon first use of the chatbot and in response to distress detected in user input;

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Texas has adopted parallel transparency requirements: SB 1188 mandates that practitioners disclose the use of AI for diagnostic purposes to patients15, while HB 149 (the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act) requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI systems, including in healthcare service contexts16.

endorsements.title: Best Practice Guidelines for Bioethical Use of Medical AI in Healthcare. An eDelphi Consensus Exercise
endorsements.quote: Patients must always know if they are dealing with a human or with an AI.

endorsements.title: Your robot therapist is not your therapist: understanding the role of AI-powered mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: One solution as suggested by Sweeney C et al. ( 11 ) is to have the chatbot present gentle reminders to users that they are not human and powered by AI to help them understand that they are not receiving therapeutic treatment from a clinician.

endorsements.title: Navigating the Ethical Landmines of ChatGPT: Implications of Intelligent Chatbots in Plastic Surgery Clinical Practice
endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
endorsements.quote: Patients must be notified that they are interacting with an automated machine.

endorsements.title: The Role of Humanization and Robustness of Large Language Models in Conversational Artificial Intelligence for Individuals With Depression: A Critical Analysis
endorsements.quote: A responsible approach involves clearly communicating to users that they are interacting with AI-based tools and what this exactly means, enabling them to make informed decisions about the assistance they receive and being aware of their limitations as well as differences from human conversation.

endorsements.title: Empowering Patient Autonomy: The Role of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Scaffolding Informed Consent in Medical Practice
endorsements.quote: It would also be important to ensure that patients understand the nature and limitations of their interaction with an AI system, the potential algorithmic biases (without undermining patient trust), and that they are engaging with technology rather than a human clinician.

endorsements.title: Expert Consensus Best Practices for the Safe, Ethical, and Effective Design and Implementation of Artificially Intelligent Conversational Agent (i.e., Chatbot/Virtual Human) Systems in Health Care Applications
endorsements.quote: We propose that all AICAs should be transparent in their identity, clearly disclosing to users—whether solicited or unsolicited depending on the context—that the interaction is with AI, not a human.

endorsements.title: AI-augmented frameworks for enhancing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials: A memory clinic perspective
endorsements.issuer: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
endorsements.quote: Additionally, generative AI’s tendency to fabricate human-like experiences (e.g., claiming personal anecdotes) poses deception risks [ 78 ], especially for vulnerable AD patients; safeguards such as disclaimers, prompt restrictions, and family oversight are essential to prevent exploitation [ 79 ].

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: For identity and autonomy, all patient-facing deployments should meet a baseline disclosure standard, including clear labeling of synthetic content, explicit affirmation that no real clinician is speaking, and an accessible opt out.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: These controls include clear communication of the system’s nonhuman identity, calibrated disclosure of uncertainty and epistemic limits, and structured redirection when users request diagnosis, prognosis, prescribing, or other clinician-dependent judgments [ 97 , 132 ].

endorsements.title: Empowering Educators to Build AI Chatbots in Health Professions Education: Tutorial on a No-Code Design Workflow
endorsements.quote: Learners should be clearly informed that they are interacting with an AI tool, that its outputs may contain inaccuracies, and that professional decision-making must always be grounded in verified evidence and supervised practice.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Humanized AI Avatars and Messenger Gender for Dental Postprocedure Instructions: Two Randomized Experiments
evidence.outcome: Effect of AI-identity disclosure on intention to comply and return to same dentist
evidence.effect: Disclosure did not change intention to follow instructions but lowered likelihood of returning to same dentist (P<.01; Cohen d 0.35 and 0.37 for disclosed humanized and disclosed animated AI vs real person).
evidence.quote: Prior disclosure that the video was AI generated resulted in a lower willingness to return to the same dentist than the real-person condition ( P <.01; Cohen d =0.35 and 0.37 for the disclosed humanized AI and disclosed animated AI conditions, respectively).

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Aid Caregivers of Pediatric Cancer Patients in Information Seeking? A Cross-Sectional Investigation
evidence.outcome: Frequency of AI disclosure in LLM responses to caregivers
evidence.effect: AI disclosure was less frequent in ChatGPT responses; Bard balanced AI disclosure with clarity. No numbers reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Regarding the disclosure of responses being generated by AI, it was observed less frequently in ChatGPT responses, which may have affected the clarity of responses, whereas Bard maintained a balance between AI disclosure and response clarity.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated responses to 26 FAQs, rated by 5 experts

commentary.bottom_line: Endorsing sources, including Utah HB 452, which makes disclosure mandatory for mental health chatbots, support AI-identity disclosure, but only one simulated trial has tested disclosure, and it did not measure whether disclosure reduces over-trust. In that trial, disclosure left intention to follow instructions unchanged and lowered intention to return to the same dentist.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=906) tested disclosure using simulated dental scenarios. Its outcomes were intentions to comply and to return, not misidentification of the agent or over-trust, so directness is poor. A single study cannot establish consistency or precision. Downgrading for indirectness and imprecision leaves the certainty of benefit for the targeted hazard very low.

The hazard study found that ChatGPT disclosed its AI identity less often than Bard when answering caregiver questions. This suggests that a model's own statements may not reliably disclose what it is. In the trial, disclosure did not change intention to follow instructions, so disclosure may not reduce reliance on advice that is wrong.

The model-to-model variation in self-disclosure suggests that deployers should not depend on the language model to announce itself. A fixed disclosure at the interface, set outside model output, may be more consistent. No study tested how disclosures should be timed, repeated after inactivity, or worded in real patient-facing workflows.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to disclose clearly and conspicuously that they are AI and not human. One commentary reports that Texas HB 149 requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI. NIST AI 600-1 advises disclosure before interaction in higher-risk contexts. For these deployments, the legal obligation applies regardless of the evidence.

Participants shown a disclosed humanized or animated AI rated themselves less likely to return to the same dentist than those shown a real person (Cohen d 0.35 and 0.37). Leaders may face some loss of patient willingness to return. The trial measured intentions, not actual return visits.

The trial suggests that patients who know they are dealing with AI may be less willing to return to the practice, although they still intended to follow its instructions. One endorsing commentary on patient-facing AI video calls for an accessible opt-out alongside disclosure, but no study tested whether an opt-out affects trust or safety.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether AI-identity disclosure, or repeating it when asked or after inactivity, reduces patients' misidentification of a chatbot as a clinician, over-trust, or harm in live clinical deployments. The one trial used simulated dental scenarios and measured intentions only.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. It is therefore unknown whether these populations understand disclosures or whether disclosures change their trust and behavior. No study tested translated or plain-language disclosures.
